summary: A humorous April Fools memo describing a protocol suite for an infinite number of monkeys at typewriters, who try to type the works of Shakespeare or a good television show. It is not a real working protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A joke document about endless monkeys typing at keyboards to see if they write a great play by accident.

subtitle: A humorous protocol suite for managing infinite monkeys at typewriters

tldr.problem: If an infinite number of monkeys sit at typewriters for long enough, they will eventually produce the complete works of Shakespeare—but how would you manage them or know when they succeeded?
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2795, an April Fools joke from April 1, 2000, proposes IMPS, a protocol suite with management protocols (KEEPER), communication protocols (CHIMP), and evaluation protocols (IAMB-PENT and PAN) for organizing monkeys, collecting their transcripts, and checking if they have typed anything worthwhile.
tldr.outcome: The document is humor, but it seriously designs protocols with real structure: packet formats, state machines, protocol numbers, and example exchanges. It parodies protocol RFCs while exploring how you might actually manage such a system.

today: RFC 2795 is an April Fools RFC, humorous and not a real protocol. It remains one of the most creative April Fools jokes ever published by the IETF. However, the engineering concepts—packet structure, state machines, protocol numbers, example exchanges—are modeled after real protocols, making it both funny and a clever parody of how RFCs are written.

sections.title: The Problem and the Joke
sections.content: This is an April Fools RFC, published April 1, 2000. The document humorously treats the famous thought experiment—that an infinite number of monkeys randomly hitting typewriter keys will eventually type Shakespeare—as an engineering problem. It asks the real questions that would arise: how do you monitor infinite monkeys? How do you collect their output? How do you recognize success? And what if a monkey produces something even better than Shakespeare, like a good television sitcom? The RFC then proposes a complete protocol suite to address these 'practical' problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if someone asked 'let us actually try this with computers and monkeys.' This document is the 'how would we do it?' answer, told as a joke that is also completely serious.

sections.title: The Architecture
sections.content: IMPS defines four key entities: ZOOs house groups of monkeys and manage their equipment; SIMIANs (Semi-Integrated, Monkey-Interfacing Anthropomorphic Nodes) are interfaces attached to individual monkeys that translate monkey behavior into network messages; BARDs (Big Annex of Reference Documents) check if transcripts match classical works like Shakespeare; and CRITICs (Collective Reviewer's Innovative Transcript Integration Center) evaluate whether new transcripts are innovative enough to publish. The IMPS packet structure includes version, sequence number, protocol number, source, destination, and data fields—just like a real protocol. Communication uses three sub-protocols: KEEPER (ZOO to SIMIAN), CHIMP (SIMIAN to ZOO), and IAMB-PENT and PAN (ZOO to evaluators).
sections.plainLanguage: The design treats monkeys as networked devices with 'managers' (ZOOs), interfaces (SIMIANs), and expert reviewers (BARD and CRITIC). It is like designing a real system, except the 'devices' are monkeys.

sections.title: The Protocols and Example
sections.content: KEEPER defines request codes (like STATUS, HEARTBEAT, WAKEUP, TYPE, FASTER, TRANSCRIPT) and response codes (ASLEEP, GONE, DISTRACTED, NORESPONSE, ALIVE, DEAD, ACCEPT, REFUSE). CHIMP defines client requests like SEND (for resources like FOOD, WATER, MEDICINE), REPLACE (typewriter, paper, monkey), CLEAN, NOTIFY, and TRANSCRIPT. The RFC includes a sample ZOO-to-SIMIAN exchange where a monkey named BoBo becomes 'distracted,' refuses to type, and leaves. Another example shows BoBo dead by morning. The IAMB-PENT protocol uses Shakespearean language (RECEIVETH, PRITHEE, REGRETTETH, ACCEPTETH) to match transcripts to classical works. The absurdist humor builds as you realize the specification is both serious and ridiculous.
sections.plainLanguage: There are real commands and response codes. One example shows a monkey refusing to work. Another shows managers sending requests in fancy Shakespearean language. Every detail is invented, but treated as a real protocol.
